_doc: Topic labels (added 2026-11-10 at Michiko's request). Each topic tags articles (by issue + headline, plus page when a headline repeats in an issue) and events (by issue + name). build_viewer.py puts a chip on every tagged entry; the chip opens a page listing everything under the topic. The Events tab search also finds a topic by its label. To add an entry, add its issue and headline/name here and rebuild. A key that matches nothing stops the build.

topics.label: Streetcar discrimination
topics.note: Exclusion of Black riders from Philadelphia's city passenger railways (streetcars), and the protests, petitions and court cases against it. Related entries on railroad cars and on other cities are included (the 1837 Broadway omnibus in New York, the West Jersey Railroad, the Pennsylvania Railroad's separate car, Havre de Grace).

timeline.title: Streetcar Discrimination in Philadelphia
timeline.intro: Black Philadelphians were fighting for the right to ride long before the streetcar. In 1837 the Colored American denounced the treatment of a Black man turned away from a New York omnibus, and in November 1840 Westward Keeling of Philadelphia bought space in the Public Ledger to protest that his 14-year-old daughter Araminta had been made to ride on top of a stagecoach in the cold. When the city's horse-drawn passenger railways began running in 1858, they refused to carry Black riders inside, or made them stand on the front platform. This timeline follows the ejections and attacks, and the organized answer to them: letters, mass meetings, petitions, lectures and court cases, through the state law of March 1867 that forbade the exclusion, and what happened after it.

phases.title: Before the war
phases.note: The fight began with omnibuses, stagecoaches and railroads, decades before the horse cars.

phases.title: 1861 and 1862
phases.note: Riders put off the cars, and the first letters and editorials in the Christian Recorder.

phases.title: 1863 and 1864
phases.note: Soldiers and their families refused, mass meetings at Sansom Street Hall and Masonic Hall, the Union League's appeal to the railway companies, and William Still's committee.

phases.title: 1865 and 1866
phases.note: The Social, Civil and Statistical Association's lecture course, petitions to the legislature, Senator Lowry's speech, and continued ejections.

phases.title: 1867: the law
phases.note: The bill passes the Senate and House and Governor Geary signs it in March. Then the first test cases and the celebrations.

phases.title: Remembered later
phases.note: Later recollections, such as William Carl Bolivar's columns in the Philadelphia Tribune.

timeline.incidents_intro: Each bar counts the separate times a Black rider was put off, refused, forced onto the platform, attacked, or made to ask the white passengers' leave to ride, as reported in the sources we have read so far. An incident reported in several issues is counted once. These are only the cases that reached print, and only in the issues read so far; the papers themselves said such treatment happened every day.

topics.label: Parades and processions
topics.note: Public parades, street processions and celebrations in which Black Philadelphians and their societies, lodges, schools and regiments marched, along with the debates over whether to march and the attacks on those who did. Entries from New York, Brooklyn, New Haven and Boston are included. Funeral processions are not listed here yet.

topics.label: Migrations
topics.note: Black Philadelphians and others leaving and arriving: emigration and removal to Haiti, to Liberia and West Africa, to Canada West, to the Pacific coast, and farther to Australia and the Caribbean, along with moves within the United States and the debates over whether to go. Entries run from the 1820s through the Civil War years, with a few later recollections.
